lecture11.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction

sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions

teaching.text: A **mass-spring system** is a mass hooked up to a spring, and the whole system can be understood by asking what each part "wants."
children: **The spring wants to be at its equilibrium position**, which is its resting length. If it is stretched or squished, it pulls or pushes to get back there.
**A mass that is moving wants to keep on moving.** Once it gets going, it does not stop on its own.

Put these two wants together and the system vibrates. When the mass is pulled out and let go, the spring pulls it back toward equilibrium, but the mass is moving when it gets there, so it **keeps on moving** past equilibrium and squishes the spring. Now the spring pushes it back the other way, the mass overshoots again, and the cycle repeats.
In real life, friction from the table slowly brings the motion to a stop. The model leaves friction out, so in the model the system vibrates forever.

teaching.text: The same system can be pictured in **two directions**, and it is important to be able to picture it both ways.
children: In the **longitudinal** picture, the motion is **left to right**, with the mass moving back and forth along the line of the spring.
In the **transverse** picture, the motion is **up and down**. The mass sits between two walls with a spring on each side, and when it is pulled up and let go, it goes up and down.

teaching.text: **Both pictures move in exactly the same way**, and they do so for the same reason.
children: In the transverse picture, pulling the mass up **stretches the springs**, and because **springs hate being extended**, they pull the mass back down.
When the mass passes the middle, the springs are not stretched at all. But the mass is moving, so **it keeps on moving** and stretches them on the other side.

So the transverse system goes through stretch and release over and over, exactly like the longitudinal one. Some systems are easier to think about longitudinally and others transversely, but both describe the same vibration.
The two versions also vibrate at the same rate, because they have the same mass and the same total stiffness.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: Two things set how fast a mass-spring system vibrates, and they are the **mass** and the **stiffness**. The number of back-and-forth cycles the system completes each second is called its **frequency**.
**A heavier mass vibrates more slowly**, and this matches everyday experience. **Heavy branches sway back and forth slowly, while little branches sway back and forth quickly.**
children: A heavy mass is hard to get moving and hard to turn around, so each trip back and forth takes longer.
Making the mass much heavier therefore makes the whole system vibrate at a noticeably lower rate.

teaching.text: **A stiffer spring makes the system vibrate faster.** Stiffness is harder to picture than mass, but the idea is that **the stiffer something is, the faster it wants to go back** to where it started.
children: A stiff spring pulls back hard, so it turns the mass around sooner.
Making the spring much stiffer therefore makes the whole system vibrate at a noticeably higher rate.

teaching.text: The two rules point in **opposite directions**. **Raising the mass lowers the frequency, and raising the stiffness raises the frequency**, and these two rules explain everything else about modes.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: With **two masses**, the system has **two walls**, a spring from each wall to a mass, and **one spring between the two masses**. All of the masses are equal and all of the springs are equal.

This system can vibrate in **two different ways**, which are called **modes**, and **a mode is just another word for a way of vibrating.** The two modes are told apart by one question, which is whether the masses are going together or going against each other.
children: In **Mode 1**, the masses move **together**. In the transverse picture, both masses are pulled up and let go, and they go up and down side by side. In the longitudinal picture, both are pulled to the left and let go, and they move left and right as a pair.

In **Mode 2**, the masses move **against each other**. One mass is pulled down and the other up, and when they are let go, one goes up whenever the other goes down. In the longitudinal picture, one is pulled left and the other right, and they move toward each other and then away from each other.

teaching.text: A system can also vibrate in **both modes at the same time**.
children: To start this, both masses are pulled up, but one is pulled higher than the other. Both start falling, which is Mode 1, but because they are uneven, the middle spring also pushes them against each other, which is Mode 2.
The result moves **together and against each other at the same time**, so sometimes both masses head the same way and sometimes they head opposite ways.
This seems strange, but real systems do it all the time, and speech production is one of them.

teaching.text: **This foundation cannot be memorized**, because each step builds on the step before it. Trying to memorize it means memorizing pages without understanding them, while following the reasoning is what makes the later material make sense.

sections.title: Pop quiz

teaching.text: The two modes have **different frequencies**. **When the masses go together, they move back and forth slowly, and when they go against each other, they move back and forth quickly.** So **Mode 2 has the higher frequency.**

This is puzzling at first, because both modes use **the same two masses and the same three springs**, so nothing about the parts has changed. The explanation comes from asking **what each spring is doing** in each mode.
children: In **both modes**, the **two outer springs** stretch and compress as the masses move.

In **Mode 1**, the two masses move together, so the **middle spring never stretches or compresses**. It just rides along with the masses, acting less like a spring and more like a rigid bar, so **effectively Mode 1 has only two springs**.
In **Mode 2**, the masses move against each other, so the **middle spring is stretched and squished** over and over. **All three springs are working**, and all three hate being stretched.

teaching.text: So Mode 2 **uses more stiffness**. **More stiffness means more pull back toward equilibrium, and more pull means a higher frequency.**
children: Nothing about the springs themselves changed, because what differs is **how each mode uses the springs**.
Mode 1 does not use the middle spring and Mode 2 does, and that one difference makes Mode 2 vibrate faster.

teaching.text: The general rule follows from this. **The more the masses go against each other, the more the springs stretch and compress, so the more stiffness the mode uses and the higher its frequency.**

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: With **three masses**, the system has **three modes**, one more than with two masses. Each mode is a different way the masses can move relative to each other.
children: In **Mode 1**, all three masses go back and forth together, and this mode has the **lowest frequency**.

In **Mode 2**, the middle mass is left untouched while the two outer masses are pulled apart. The two outer ones move against each other, the **middle one does not move at all**, and this mode has the **middle frequency**.
In **Mode 3**, the middle mass moves **opposite to the two outer masses**, and this mode has the **highest frequency**. It is easiest to see in the transverse picture.

teaching.text: The frequencies follow the same reasoning as with two masses.
children: **Mode 1 is very slow** because the masses move together, so the **two middle springs do nothing**. Their job is to stretch and compress, which is what raises frequency, and when they just ride along, they add no stiffness.
In **Mode 2**, the springs do stretch and compress, but not as much as they could.
In **Mode 3**, **everything is going against everything else**. That means **lots of stretching and lots of compression**, which uses the most stiffness, so Mode 3 moves fastest.
The masses and springs are the same in all three modes, so **only the way the masses move relative to each other changes the frequency.**

teaching.text: All three modes can also happen **at the same time**, so the masses move together, against each other and middle against the sides all at once. However the system is started, it vibrates as some mix of its pure modes.
Exciting some modes and not others is a real skill.
children: **Learning a musical instrument means learning how to make the masses and springs vibrate in certain modes and not others.** How a string is plucked or a violin is bowed decides which modes get excited, and these favored modes are heard as **notes**.
**A trained singer** does the same thing with the vocal folds, controlling their mass and stiffness to carry a tune.

teaching.text: The same logic continues with **four masses**, which give four modes. All four can go together, the two on the left can go against the two on the right, the two in the middle can go against the two outer ones, or every mass can go against its neighbors.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: The pattern holds for any number of masses, so **N masses give N modes.** One mass has only one way to vibrate, two masses have two, three masses have three, and so on.
children: Moving up to higher modes, **more parts move against each other**, so the pattern has **more reversals** in it.
More parts moving against each other means more stretching, so **higher modes have higher frequencies**.
In chains of separate masses like these, the mode frequencies are generally **not whole-number multiples** of the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: Comparing the same mode across chains of different lengths reveals a shared pattern.
children: **Every Mode 1 is alike**, because all the masses go up and down together.
**Every Mode 2 is alike**, because the **left side goes against the right side**. With only two masses, that simply means one against the other.
**Every Mode 3 is alike**, because the **middle goes against the sides**.

teaching.text: Packing in more and more masses and springs, all the way to an **infinite number**, gives a **string**, like a guitar or piano string. Every little piece of a string has mass, and every little piece stretches like a spring, so a string vibrates in all the same kinds of modes.
children: In the **lowest mode**, the whole string goes up and down together, with hardly any stretching between its pieces, and that mode gives the **lowest note**.
In **higher modes**, more and more parts of the string move against each other.
A string plucked without any skill vibrates in many modes at once.

teaching.text: A system can also be **fixed on one side and free to sway on the other**. A **building** is like this, because it is fixed to the ground at the bottom and free to sway at the top in high winds or earthquakes.
children: Civil engineers design buildings to sway in **Mode 1**, with everything moving together, and never in higher modes, where floors would move against each other.
A building is not made so stiff that it cannot move at all. Instead it is designed to sway safely in its lowest mode.
The same vocabulary of modes describes music, buildings and, as the system builds up, speech.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A **string fixed at both ends** vibrates in many modes. In the lowest mode the whole string goes up and down together, and each higher mode has more sections moving against each other and **completes more cycles in the same amount of time**. Frequency is measured in **Hertz**, which means **times per second**.
children: For a string fixed at both ends, each mode is a **whole-number multiple** of the lowest one, so the second mode is twice the lowest, the third is three times the lowest, and so on. Modes that line up this way are called **consecutive harmonics**.
The motion in the animation is slowed way down so that it can be followed by eye.

teaching.text: A real string vibrates in **all of its modes at the same time**. Adding the separate motions together at every point gives one complicated, changing shape, and that combined motion is what an actual plucked string does.
The **spectrum** of a sound tells **which frequencies are in it and how much of each there is**.
children: For a string moving in five modes at once, the spectrum has **five spikes**, one at the frequency of each moving mode.

If the string vibrated **only in Mode 3**, there would be no movement in the other modes, so the spectrum would have **just one spike, at the frequency of Mode 3**. That pattern is like a **one-hot encoding**, with one active slot and all the others at zero.
So the spectrum turns a complicated motion into a simple list of which modes are moving and how strongly.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: **The vocal folds are even more complicated than strings.** They are a bunch of muscle forming a surface, which is called a **membrane**, so their masses and springs are spread across two directions instead of along one line. The same logic of modes still applies to them.
children: In **Mode 1**, all of the masses go up and down together.
In **Mode 2**, the **left half goes against the right half**.
In **Mode 3**, the **middle is stuck** while the sides go against each other.
In **Mode 4**, four sections go against each other, and the patterns get more and more complicated in still higher modes.

teaching.text: The frequencies given to the membrane's modes in the picture are assigned for teaching, not worked out for that rectangle. In real vocal folds, **all the modes happen at the same time**, so producing voice makes the vocal folds vibrate in many modes at once, and that creates a spectrum full of spikes.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: **The scientific method** depends on **very clear statements about how systems work**, and these are usually written as **differential equations**, which describe how quantities change over time.
children: The simple spring equation is one example. Solving it predicts that if the spring is pulled it goes back, and if it is pushed it also goes back.
**Solving the equations gives a prediction** about how the world will behave **when it is actually measured**.

teaching.text: For the voice, the reasoning moves from a theory to a prediction.
children: The theory is that **the vocal folds are a membrane** built from many masses and springs, and that when they vibrate, they do so in many modes at once.

The equations for the vocal folds are the same type as the spring equations, only more of them and **slightly more complicated**, so the intuition built from masses and springs is enough to reason with.
The prediction is that **if anyone's laryngeal vibration signal is measured, its spectrum will have evenly spaced spikes.** These evenly spaced spikes are called **harmonics**.

teaching.text: **The prediction was tested in class.** Two students each made a sound with the **mouth wide open**, so that no particular vowel was being made, and the spectrum of each voice was examined in **Praat**, a program for analyzing speech.
children: In the first student's voice, the spikes came at a low frequency and its multiples, **evenly spaced** just as predicted.
In the second student's voice, the first spike was about twice as high, and the following spikes were again **evenly spaced**, only farther apart.
**The prediction held for both voices**, so a prediction built from simple masses and springs turned out to be precise and real.

teaching.text: The difference between the two voices follows from the mass rule.
children: The second student's voice has a **higher pitch**, so their vocal folds are probably **smaller and thinner**.
**Thinner folds have less mass, and less mass means a higher frequency**, so the first harmonic is higher and every harmonic after it is spaced farther apart.

teaching.text: This is part of how we **recognize people by their voices**. Each person's vocal folds produce their own spectrum, and becoming familiar with someone means becoming familiar with the spectrum of their voice. How a person says particular vowels also matters, but that depends on the vibration of the **air** above the vocal folds, not on the folds themselves.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A string can also be **fixed at one end and free at the other**, just like the building that is fixed to the ground and sways at the top. This string is **fixed at the bottom** and **free at the top**.
children: The **fixed bottom** cannot move, and a point that never moves is called a **node**.
The **free top** moves the most, and a point of largest motion is called an **antinode**.
So every mode has to start with a node at the bottom and end with an antinode at the top.

teaching.text: This changes which modes are possible. **Only the odd harmonics occur**, meaning one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency. The modes at two times and four times the lowest are missing, because those patterns cannot end with free motion at the top.
children: **Mode 1** has no still point inside the string, so its motion grows steadily from the fixed bottom to the free top, like a building swaying as a whole.
Each higher mode adds more still points inside the string, with more sections swinging against each other.
When all four modes are excited equally, the spectrum measured at the free end has **four equal spikes**.

teaching.text: Freeing one end also lowers the whole system. For a string of the **same length and the same wave speed**, switching from **fixed at both ends** to **fixed at one end and free at the other** **halves the lowest frequency**.
The contrast between the two strings comes down to what happens at the ends.
children: When **both ends are fixed**, the string has **every whole-number multiple** of the lowest frequency.
When **one end is fixed and the other is free**, the string has **only the odd multiples**.

lecture12.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization

teaching.text: This year's **Nobel Prize in economics** went to work on the **microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization**. **Stabilization** means getting a system to **equilibrium and keeping it there**, which is the same **balancing feedback** a spring has, since a spring that is pulled or pushed always goes back to equilibrium.

The prize was described as work on **boom-bust cycles**, the economy's swings between good times and bad times. In that picture, **unemployment and inflation go in reverse of each other**, rising and falling like two oscillating curves.
children: These are the same two curves found in a mass-spring system. One curve starts big, becomes negative and then becomes positive again, and that curve is **x**, the position. The other curve is its flip, which is **v**, the velocity.

In the economy, **inflation plays the part of x and unemployment plays the part of v**, so the math and the concept are exactly the same as for masses and springs, just in a completely different domain.

teaching.text: The winning theory is called **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, and each part of its name connects to masses, springs and gradient descent.
children: The word **dynamic** says that the theory describes how the economy **changes over time**.

The word **stochastic** says that the theory handles **shocks**, which are things that happen unpredictably, like a war starting or a factory burning down. This works like **stochastic gradient descent**, which gets knocked off course by one wildly off number but comes back to the average as it keeps learning, and in the same way the economic model returns toward balance after a shock.

The words **general equilibrium** say that the goal is an economy that **does not jump around** but settles into balance, and **stabilization policy** tries to **damp** the swings, making the oscillations smaller and smaller.

**Micro** refers to individual decisions, like buying something or applying for a job, while **macro** refers to whole-economy quantities like inflation and unemployment. Speech has the same structure, because many tiny oscillations in the mouth add up to a meaning that a listener understands without tracking each oscillation.

teaching.text: **The same idea explains how economies work, how butterflies fly, how music works and how speech works.** Understanding one idea that runs across many domains is the kind of imagination that matters far more than memorizing.

sections.title: One mass, two directions

teaching.text: A mass-spring system rests on two facts, which are that **the spring wants to be at its equilibrium position** and that **a moving mass keeps on moving**. When the mass is pulled and let go, the spring pulls it back, the mass overshoots because it keeps moving, and so the system vibrates.

The same system can be pictured **longitudinally**, with the mass moving **left and right**, or **transversely**, with the mass moving **up and down** between two springs. **Both pictures move in exactly the same way** and at the same rate. Both views matter, because one will help with the vocal folds and the other will help with the air in the vocal tract.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: **Raising the mass lowers the frequency, and raising the stiffness raises the frequency.**
children: A heavier mass is harder to turn around, so the system goes back and forth **fewer times per second**.
A stiffer spring pulls back harder, so the system goes back and forth **more times per second**.
Both rules hold whether the system is pictured longitudinally or transversely.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: With two masses, the system can vibrate in **two modes**. A **mode** is a way of vibrating, and the two modes here are defined by whether the masses go **together** or **against each other**.
children: In **Mode 1**, both masses are lifted and let go, and they go up and down **together**.
In **Mode 2**, one mass is pulled up and the other down, and they go **against each other**.
When both are lifted but one higher than the other, **both modes happen at the same time**, so the masses go up and down together while also going against each other.

teaching.text: **Mode 1 is slow and Mode 2 is fast**, even though both use the same masses and the same three springs. The difference is **how many springs are actually working** in each mode.
children: In **Mode 1**, the **middle spring never stretches or compresses**. It moves along like a rigid bar, so it is not behaving like a spring at all, and **effectively Mode 1 has only two springs.**
In **Mode 2**, **all three springs stretch and compress**, so **effectively Mode 2 has three springs.**
**More springs working means more stiffness, and more stiffness means a higher frequency**, because the stiffer the system is, the faster it has to go back to equilibrium.

teaching.text: So **multiple masses give multiple modes, each with its own frequency.** The higher the mode, the more springs it uses, and the higher its frequency.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: With **three masses**, there are **three modes**.
children: In **Mode 1**, all three masses go back and forth **together**. The springs hardly stretch, so the stiffness in use is low and the frequency is the **lowest**.
In **Mode 2**, the **middle mass stays frozen** while the two outer masses go **against each other** around it. There is more stretching and compression, so the frequency is higher.
In **Mode 3**, **all three masses go against each other.** This mode has the **most stretching and compression**, so its frequency is the **highest**.

teaching.text: Changing a single part of the system affects each mode differently, depending on what that part is doing in that mode.
**Making the middle spring stiffer** affects only the modes that actually stretch it.
children: **Mode 1 stays the same**, because in Mode 1 the middle spring never stretches or compresses, so its stiffness does not matter.
**Mode 2 rises**, because in Mode 2 the middle spring is stretched and squished, so a stiffer spring pulls harder and the mode speeds up.
The more stiffness is packed into that one spring, the more Mode 2 rises, while Mode 1 never changes at all.

teaching.text: **Making the middle mass heavier** affects only the modes in which that mass moves.
children: **Mode 1 goes down**, because the middle mass moves in Mode 1, so making it heavier slows the system.
**Mode 2 stays the same**, because the middle mass is frozen in Mode 2, and **a mass that does not move has no effect on frequency**, no matter how heavy it gets.

**Mode 3 goes down, and it goes down more than Mode 1 does**, because the middle mass moves even more in Mode 3 than in Mode 1, and **the more a mass moves, the more its weight affects the frequency**.

teaching.text: The general rule is that **a mass's influence on frequency depends on how much it moves.** If it does not move at all it has no effect, if it moves a little it has a little effect, and if it moves a lot it has a big effect. These principles cannot be memorized as a list, because each one is worked out by asking what the part is doing in that mode.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: Adding masses keeps the same patterns, so **one mass has one mode**, two masses have two, three have three, and so on. The modes repeat the same ideas as the chain gets longer.
children: **Every Mode 1 is the same idea**, with everything going up and down together.
**Every Mode 2 divides the system into two parts**, one going up while the other goes down, and if the number of masses is odd, the middle one is frozen.
**Every Mode 3 divides the system into three parts**, with the sides going up while the middle goes down.
Lower modes go up and down slowly because the system is not using much stiffness there, and higher modes go faster because more springs are stretching and compressing.

teaching.text: Packing in more and more masses and springs gives a **string**, like a guitar or piano string, because a string is an **infinite number of masses and springs**. Every little piece of a string has weight, which is its mass, and every little piece hates being stretched or compressed, which is its springiness.
children: In the **first mode**, the whole string goes up and down together.
In the **second mode**, the two halves go against each other.
In the **third mode**, the middle goes against the sides.
In musical instruments, these mode frequencies are heard as **notes**.

teaching.text: A real string vibrates in **many modes at the same time**, so its motion is the **sum of all the modes**. Hearing just a single mode would be a very annoying sound called a **pure tone**, like an ambulance siren, because real sounds have many modes together.
**The ear can tell many instruments apart at once** because the ear is itself made of masses and springs that are well matched to the masses and springs vibrating in the world.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: The modes of a **string fixed at both ends** are **harmonics**, which means they are **exact multiples of the base frequency**, the frequency of the lowest mode.
The multiples come from **how many copies of the first mode fit into each higher mode.**
children: The **first mode** is a single bump that goes up and down.
The **second mode** fits **two** of those bumps, one going up while the other goes down, so it vibrates **twice as fast**.
The **third mode** fits **three** bumps, so it vibrates **three times as fast**, and the pattern continues the same way for every higher mode.
So **the frequency of each mode is the base frequency multiplied by how many times the first mode fits into the whole string.**

teaching.text: The **spectrum** tells **which frequencies a vibration has and how much amplitude is in each one**, with frequency running along one axis and amplitude, the amount of vibration, along the other.
children: This string's spectrum has a spike at each harmonic, because all of the modes are added together.
Because many frequencies happen at once, the actual motion looks **erratic**, much like the waveform of speech.
Measured at one marked point, the spikes come out **equal**, because each mode's strength was set to give the same size at that point.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: Everything so far can be summed up as a short list of principles, and each one comes from the same two facts, that mass resists being turned around and that springs hate being stretched.

**Raising the mass makes the frequency go down, and raising the stiffness makes the frequency go up.** One line of the printed list says that stiffness lowers frequency, but that line is a typo, and the stiffness principle further down the same list correctly says that stiffness raises frequency.

**A system of N masses has N modes of vibration, and each mode has a higher frequency than the one before.** Two masses can go together or against each other, so they have two modes, and three masses have three.
**Increasing a mass lowers frequency in proportion to how much that mass moves, and how much it moves depends on where it is.**
children: A mass that does **not move** has **no effect**, however heavy it gets. At the very edges of a string there is no motion, so adding mass there changes nothing.
A mass that **moves a lot** lowers the frequency **a lot**. In the middle of the first, third and fifth modes there is lots of motion, so adding mass there drops the frequency a lot.

teaching.text: **Where there is maximal movement there is no stretching, and where there is maximal stretching there is no movement.**
**Increasing a spring's stiffness raises frequency in proportion to how much that spring stretches and compresses**, which also depends on where it is.
children: Where there is **no stretching or compression**, stiffening the spring has **no effect**.
Where there is **lots of stretching and compression**, stiffening it raises the frequency **a lot**.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: On a vibrating string, **the places with the most movement and the places with the most stretching are not the same places.**
children: In the **lowest mode**, the **most movement is in the middle**, where the string just goes up and down without being stretched.
The **most stretching is at the sides**, near the fixed ends, where the string barely moves at all.

teaching.text: In higher modes, the same alternation repeats over and over along the string.
children: A stretch with **lots of movement and no stretching** is followed by a stretch with **lots of stretching and no movement**, and then by **lots of movement** again, and so on along the string.
So **where there is the most movement there is the least stretching, and where there is the most stretching there is the least movement.**
This alternation does not have to be memorized, because it can be worked out by watching what each piece of the string is doing.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently

teaching.text: On a string, one small section is marked where **Mode 4 is moving a lot** while **Mode 5 has no motion at all but lots of stretching**. Raising **both the mass and the stiffness** of that section has a different effect on each mode, and each effect has to be reasoned out separately.
**For Mode 4**, the section is mostly moving.
children: **Raising the mass lowers the frequency**, because the mass is moving there.
**Raising the stiffness has no effect**, because the string there is just moving up and down without stretching or compressing.
So **the frequency of Mode 4 goes down**.

teaching.text: **For Mode 5**, the section is mostly stretching.
children: **Raising the mass has no effect**, because there is no motion there.
**Raising the stiffness raises the frequency**, because there is lots of stretching there.
So **the frequency of Mode 5 goes up**.

teaching.text: **Increasing both the stiffness and the mass at that one spot lowers the frequency of Mode 4 and raises the frequency of Mode 5.** The same principles get applied again and again. **Where there is no motion, added stiffness raises frequency, and where there is motion, added mass lowers frequency.**

This method of changing one small part and predicting the effect is called **perturbation**. It was first worked out with **drums**, which are also an infinite number of masses and springs, by a scientist who added **wax**, and so added mass, to different parts of a drum.
children: Adding wax where the drum vibrated the most made the frequency **drop**.
Adding wax where there was no motion had **no effect** on the frequency.
He heard these differences with his own ears, long before cameras could capture the motion.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: **The larynx is a whole membrane**, a surface built from many masses and springs, a bit like a **drum**. It has many modes of vibration, and they follow the same patterns as before.
children: In **Mode 1**, all of the masses go up and down together.
In **Mode 2**, the left half goes against the right half.
In **Mode 3**, the middle is stuck while the sides go against each other.
The **higher modes** divide the surface into more and more parts.

teaching.text: Just like the string, the membrane's modes are given frequencies that are multiples of the lowest one, and these values are assigned for teaching rather than worked out for that rectangle. Adding all of the motions together gives the combined surface, and its spectrum has **equal spikes**, one for each mode.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: **The scientific method depends on very clear theories** about how the world works, which are usually written as **differential equations**. **Solving the equations gives a prediction** of what will be found when the world is actually measured.
The theory and the prediction for the voice both follow from masses and springs.
children: The theory is that **the vocal folds are a membrane**, so when they vibrate, **their spectrum will have evenly spaced spikes**, which are called **harmonics**.
The differential equations are the same kind as before, only **slightly more complicated**.
The prediction is that **any laryngeal vibration signal will have a spectrum with evenly spaced harmonics.**

teaching.text: **The experiment** checks this in **Praat** by taking a spectral slice of a voice.
children: The second spike comes out at **about double** the first, and the third comes out at **about triple** the first.
So the spikes come out **evenly spaced**, exactly as predicted. Every person's voice has its own base frequency, but the spikes are always multiples of it.

teaching.text: The same reasoning explains how **smoking changes the voice**.
children: Heavy smokers can develop **nodules** on their vocal folds, and a nodule is like **adding a little mass** to one spot.
Even without a full nodule, smoking changes the **stiffness and mass of different parts** of the folds.
Those local changes shift different modes by different amounts, just like the wax on the drum, so **some harmonics stop being perfect multiples** of the base frequency and the voice sounds different.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **building** is a system that is **fixed on one side and free on the other**, because it is fixed to the earth at the bottom while the top can sway.
children: Structural engineers design buildings to absorb high winds and earthquakes by swaying in **Mode 1**, with the whole building going back and forth together.
They design them **never to vibrate in higher modes**, where one floor would go one way and the next floor the other way, because that would be far worse.
Choosing the materials and structure of each floor so that the building favors only Mode 1 is a big part of structural engineering.

teaching.text: **The air inside the vocal tract** is also fixed on one side and free on the other.
children: At the **bottom**, at the vocal folds, the **air cannot move**, because the vocal folds are closed and the air is stuck there.
At the **top**, at the lips, the air can move **in and out easily**.

Unlike a building, the air in the vocal tract **vibrates in all its modes**. Speaking changes the masses and springs of different parts of the tract, and that is how listeners know which vowel, consonant and word is being said.

teaching.text: A system fixed at one end and free at the other has a **different spectrum**, because its frequencies jump by **odd multiples** of the base frequency instead of climbing through every multiple. The reason again comes from **how many copies of the first mode fit** into each higher mode.
children: The **first mode** goes from **no motion** at the fixed end to **lots of motion** at the free end.
The **second mode** fits **three** of those pieces that run from no motion to lots of motion, so it is **three times** the base frequency.
The **third mode** fits **five** of them, so it is **five times** the base frequency.
The pieces always come in **odd numbers**, because the system must always start with no motion at the fixed end and finish with lots of motion at the free end.

teaching.text: The same holds for a string fixed at the bottom and free at the top, where **only the odd harmonics occur**. The fixed bottom is a **node**, a point with no motion, and the free top is an **antinode**, a point of largest motion. For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end **halves the lowest frequency**.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract is modeled as a **mass-spring chain that is fixed at one end and free at the other**. The **masses** stand for the **air's inertia** and the **springs** stand for its **springiness**, and the chain is **fixed at the glottis** and **free at the lips**, with **identical masses** in a **uniform tube**.
The first two modes matter most for vowels.
children: **Mode 1 corresponds to F1**, the **lowest air mode** of the tube. Its motion is still at the glottis and grows toward the lips.
**Mode 2 corresponds to F2**, the **next air mode**, and it vibrates **three times faster** than Mode 1.
**F1 and F2** are called **formants**, and they are the **resonances of the air in the vocal tract**.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: Vowels differ in the **shape of the vocal tract**, which MRI images of five vowels seen from the side make visible. **High and low** describe tongue height, while **front, central and back** describe how far forward the tongue is, and together they place a **constriction**, which is a narrowing of the tract.
children: In **Dean**, the tongue is **high and front**, which makes a **constriction about two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
In **Dune**, the tongue is **high and back**, and the vowel has a **constriction at the lips**.
In **Done**, the tongue is **central**, and the tract has **no constriction** at all.
In **Don**, the tongue is **low and back**, which makes a **constriction about one third of the way from the glottis**.
In **Dan**, the tongue is **low and front**, and no constriction position is marked for it.

teaching.text: These spots match the marks on the air chain, so each vowel's constriction lands on a different part of each air mode.

sections.title: Blank source page
Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: Three spots are marked along the tube, measured from the glottis toward the lips. The spot **one third of the way** up is labeled **/a/**, the spot **two thirds of the way** up is labeled **/i/**, and the **lip end** is labeled **/u/**.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: For **/u/**, the masses near the **lips get heavier**, which is called **loading the free end**.
**Motion dominates at the lips in both modes**, because the lip end moves a lot in Mode 1 and also in Mode 2.
Added mass where the air moves a lot slows the vibration, so **both F1 and F2 go down**.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is about **two thirds** of the way from the glottis.
children: In **Mode 1**, **the motion of the mass dominates** at that spot, so the added mass wins and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, **springiness dominates** at that spot, so the added stiffness wins and **F2 goes up**.

teaching.text: This is the same logic as Modes 4 and 5 on the string. One local change lowers one mode and raises another, because the spot **moves** in one mode and **stretches** in the other.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is about **one third** of the way from the glottis.
children: In **Mode 1**, **springiness dominates** at that spot, so **F1 goes up**.
In **Mode 2**, **the motion of the mass dominates** at that spot, so **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: The result is **the reverse of /i/**. The rule never changes, since dominant stiffness raises a formant and dominant mass lowers it, and what changes which effect wins is where the constriction sits.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: **In a system fixed at both ends, the harmonics are whole-number multiples of the base frequency**, because the base mode fits a whole number of times into each successive mode.
**In a system fixed at one end and free at the other, the harmonics are odd multiples of the base frequency**, because the base mode fits an **odd number of times** into each successive mode.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: The air moves **lengthwise**, back and forth along the tube. When neighboring bits of air move toward each other, the air between them is **compressed**, and when they move apart, it **expands**.

Watching the air in the tube makes this visible. In the uniform tube for **schwa** and in the separate rows for **Mode 1, Mode 2 and Mode 3**, some places have air **moving a lot** and other places have air **compressing a lot**, and the two alternate along the tube. That alternation is why one constriction can push two formants in opposite directions.

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: The first principle is the simplest one. **As mass goes up, frequency goes down, and as stiffness goes up, frequency goes up.** A heavier mass is harder to turn around, so it vibrates more slowly, and a stiffer spring pulls back harder, so it vibrates faster.

That principle by itself invites a **false argument**. Suppose something raises **both the mass and the stiffness** of a system. Since raising mass lowers frequency and raising stiffness raises it, it can seem that **the two effects cancel out** and nothing audible changes.
children: That reasoning is **only true of a system with a single mass**, where more mass and more stiffness really can cancel.
**In a system with many masses and springs, the effects do not cancel**, and the reason is a fact about where things happen along the system.

teaching.text: **The places with the most motion are the places with the least springiness, and the places with the most springiness have the least motion.** So the location of a change decides which of the two effects counts.
children: At a spot on a string with **no movement but lots of stretching and compression**, making the spot heavier does **nothing**, because a mass only matters if it is moving. Making it stiffer **raises** the frequency, because that spot is stretching and compressing, so raising both there makes the frequency **go up**.

At a spot with **lots of movement but no stretching**, where the string just rides up and down, making the spot heavier **lowers** the frequency, because the mass is moving a lot. Making it stiffer does **almost nothing**, because the spring there is not stretching, so raising both there makes the frequency **go down**.

teaching.text: It is even possible to raise both mass and stiffness and get **no effect at all**. That happens inside our own speech, at a constriction placed where neither effect matters.
The rest of the principles build on the first one, and **they all interact with each other**. Each idea is simple, and each one follows from what masses and springs do.

**A system with N masses has N modes of vibration, and each mode has a higher frequency than the last.** Two masses can go together or against each other, which gives two modes. Higher modes have higher frequencies because **more springs are active**, since more masses are going against each other and so the springs stretch and compress more.
**Increasing a mass lowers frequency in proportion to how much that mass moves, and how much it moves depends on where it is.**
children: If the mass is **not moving**, increasing it has **no effect at all**.
If the mass is **moving a lot**, increasing it **lowers the frequency a lot**.
If the mass is moving only a little, the frequency drops only a little.

teaching.text: **Increasing a spring's stiffness raises frequency in proportion to how much the spring stretches and compresses, and that also depends on where it is.**
children: Near places with **no motion**, there is lots of stretching and compression, so added stiffness has a **huge** effect on raising the frequency.
In places with **lots of motion**, there is no springiness in use, so added stiffness has **no** effect.

teaching.text: **Where there is maximal movement there is no stretching, and where there is maximal stretching there is no movement.** This principle ties the mass principle and the stiffness principle together, because it decides where mass matters and where stiffness matters.
The last two principles are about what happens at the ends of the system.
children: **In a system fixed at both ends, the harmonics are whole-number multiples of the base frequency**, because the base mode fits a whole number of times into each successive mode.
**In a system fixed at one end and free at the other, the formants are odd multiples of the base frequency**, because the base mode fits an **odd number of times** into each successive mode.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: Chains with anywhere from **one mass up to six masses** all follow the same rule, which is that **N masses give N independent modes**. Each chain has **fixed ends, equal masses and equal springs**, and each row of the figure lays out every mode of its chain.
Moving up to higher modes, **the pattern has more reversals and a higher vibration frequency.**
children: In the **lowest mode**, all the masses move together and the springs barely stretch, so the frequency is low.
In the **highest mode**, every mass moves against its neighbor, so every spring is working and the frequency is highest.
In chains of separate masses like these, the frequencies are generally **not whole-number multiples** of the lowest one.

sections.title: Why fixed–fixed frequencies are integer multiples

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** are the main system in speech that is **fixed on its edges**. They sit right behind the Adam's apple and form a **membrane** of many masses and springs that is **fixed on all sides**. They vibrate in modes where the masses go up and down together, or where half go up while half go down, and so on into more complicated patterns.
**The vibrations of a system fixed on its edges are called harmonics.**
children: The lowest one is the **base frequency**, which belongs to the lowest mode.

Each following harmonic is a **multiple** of the base, so the second harmonic is twice the base, the third is three times the base, and so on. Frequency is measured in **Hertz**, which means times per second.
The base frequency is different for different people, but whatever it is, the harmonics above it are always its multiples.

teaching.text: The multiples come from **counting how many copies of the first mode fit into each higher mode.**
children: On a string fixed at both ends, the first mode is **half a wave**, with one section going up and down.
The **second mode** has **two** of those sections, one going up while the other goes down, so it vibrates twice as fast as the first.
The **fifth mode** has **five** sections, so it vibrates five times as fast as the first.

Each piece from one still point to the next is called a **half-wave packet**. The first mode holds one packet, the second holds two, and so on, so **higher harmonics fit more half-wave packets into the same length.**

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A **string fixed at both ends** vibrates in all of its modes **at once**, so its combined motion is the sum of all of them. Measured at one point, its spectrum has **equal spikes**, one for each mode, because each mode's strength was set to give the same size at that point.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a flat surface **fixed on all of its edges**, and its modes are named with **two numbers** that count its moving regions in each direction.
children: In the **(1, 1)** mode, one region rises and falls as a whole.
In the **(2, 1)** and **(1, 2)** modes, two regions go against each other, along one direction or the other.
In the **(2, 2)** mode, four regions alternate with each other.
In the **(3, 1)** mode, three regions go against each other along one direction.

teaching.text: The same counting works on the membrane. The first mode fits into the second mode **twice**, so the second vibrates twice as fast, and it fits into the fourth mode **four times**, so the fourth vibrates four times as fast. The frequencies given to the five modes in the picture are assigned for teaching rather than worked out for this rectangle. The **combined surface** is the exact sum of all five motions, and its spectrum at a pickup point has **five equal spikes**.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **building** is **fixed on one side**, at the ground, and **free on the other**, at the top.
children: Engineers want it to sway in **Mode 1**, all together, which is mildly annoying on a high floor but safe.
A higher mode, with **some floors going one way and others going the other way**, would shatter the structure.

teaching.text: A system fixed at one end and free at the other has a **different counting rule**. When both ends are fixed, the basic piece runs from no motion, to lots of motion, and back to no motion. When one end is free, the basic piece runs only **from no motion to lots of motion**, with no still point at the free end.
children: The next mode up fits **three** of those pieces, so its frequency is three times the first.
The mode after that fits **five** of them, so its frequency is five times the first.
The pieces always come in **odd numbers**, so the frequencies are **odd multiples** of the first.

teaching.text: **The frequencies of a system fixed at one end and free at the other are called formants**, which is a different name from harmonics.
children: **Formants are the frequencies of vibration of a system fixed on one side and completely free on the other.**
**Their major property is that they are odd multiples of the first formant**, so they go one, three, five, seven and nine times the first, and so on.

teaching.text: **The big, important system of this kind in speech is the air in the vocal tract.** Its vibration makes all the vowels and consonants of speech, and speech works by **changing the stiffness and mass in different parts of the vocal tract**, which moves the formants.

A **building** is fixed on one side at the ground and free on the other at the top. Engineers want it to sway in the first mode, all together, which is mildly annoying on a high floor but safe. A higher mode, with some floors going one way and others going the other way, would shatter the structure.

A fixed-free system has a **different counting rule**. A fixed-fixed system's basic piece goes from nothing to lots of motion and back to nothing, while a fixed-free system's basic piece goes from nothing to lots of motion, with no still point at the free end.
If the first mode is 100 Hz, the next mode fits three of those pieces, so it is 300 Hz, and the third fits five, so it is 500 Hz.
The frequencies of a fixed-free system are called **formants**, and their major property is that they are **odd multiples** of the first.

The string fixed at the bottom and free at the top has a **node** at the fixed end, a point with no motion, and an **antinode** at the free end, a point of largest motion. Its four modes are at 100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz, so only odd harmonics occur.
For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end halves the lowest frequency, so this string was retuned to keep its lowest mode at 100 Hz.
The big, important fixed-free system in speech is the air in the vocal tract, whose vibration makes all the vowels and consonants.

sections.title: Why fixed–free frequencies are odd multiples

teaching.text: A **string fixed at the bottom and free at the top** follows the rule for one fixed end and one free end.
children: The **fixed bottom** cannot move, so it is a **node**, which is a point with no motion.
The **free top** moves the most, so it is an **antinode**, which is a point of largest motion.
So **only the odd harmonics occur** on this string.
For the **same length and wave speed**, freeing one end **halves the lowest frequency**.

teaching.text: The basic piece from a node to an antinode is called a **quarter-wave packet**, and each mode holds an **odd number** of them.
children: **Mode 1** holds just **one packet**, and **Mode 2** holds **three packets**.
**Mode 3** holds **five packets**, and **Mode 4** holds **seven packets**.

teaching.text: The counts skip the even numbers because of what has to happen at the ends.
children: Adding just **one** packet would leave a **node** at the free top, and that is not allowed.
Adding **two** packets at a time keeps the **antinode** at the top.
So **one fixed end and one free end give only odd multiples**, while **two fixed ends give every multiple**.

sections.title: Count quarter-waves from the boundary conditions

teaching.text: The basic piece from a node to an antinode is a **quarter-wave packet**, and each fixed-free mode holds an odd number of them. The first mode holds one packet, the second holds three, the third holds five and the fourth holds seven.
The counts skip the even numbers because of the ends. Adding one packet would leave a node at the free top, which is not allowed, but adding two packets keeps the antinode at the top.
So one fixed end and one free end give only odd multiples, while two fixed ends give every multiple.
In both cases, more packets in the same length means shorter waves and higher frequencies.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract can be modeled as a **chain of masses and springs that is fixed at one end and free at the other**, the same as any other vibrating system. The **masses** stand for the air's inertia, its tendency to keep moving, and the **springs** stand for its springiness when squeezed. The chain is **fixed at one end**, where there is no motion, and **completely free at the other**, and while masses and springs are easier to see than air, the model and the air itself behave the same way.
The first two modes are the ones that matter most.
children: **Mode 1 corresponds to F1**, the **lowest air mode** of the tube. Its motion is still at the fixed end and grows toward the free end.

**Mode 2 corresponds to F2**, the next mode up. It fits **three** of the pieces that run from no motion to lots of motion, while Mode 1 fits only one, so in a **uniform tube** Mode 2 vibrates **three times faster** than Mode 1.
The letter **F stands for formant**, so F1 is the first formant and F2 is the second.

teaching.text: Three spots are marked along the tube, measured from the fixed end. The spot **one third of the way** up is labeled **/a/**, the spot **two thirds of the way** up is labeled **/i/**, and the **free end** is labeled **/u/**, and each spot takes part in both modes.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: The air inside the mouth is **fixed at the vocal folds and free at the lips**.
children: At the **vocal folds**, the folds are closed, so the air **cannot go back and forth**. It is stuck there, which makes that end **fixed**.
At the **lips**, the mouth is open, so the air **goes back and forth freely**, which makes that end **free**. Air that goes out also comes back in, just as a mass goes back and forth.
Each blue circle in the figure stands for billions of air molecules.

teaching.text: Two kinds of motion tell the masses and the springs apart.
children: Where neighboring lines of air **come really close together and then move really far apart**, the air is **stretching and compressing**, and that is a sign of **springiness**.
Where the lines of air **just move back and forth together** without their spacing changing, the air is acting as a **mass**.
The easiest place to see pure mass is the **free end at the lips**, because the air there just moves back and forth with no compression at all.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: Vowels differ in **where the air is squeezed** in the vocal tract. A **constriction** is a place where the tongue or lips narrow the passage and **squeeze the air**.
children: **Done** has **no constriction**, so the airflow is **unimpeded** everywhere and the tract is open evenly along its length.

**Dean** is a **high front** vowel, and it squeezes the air under the roof of the mouth, **two thirds of the way from the glottis**. The **glottis** is the tiny space between the vocal folds, at the fixed end.
**Don** is a **low back** vowel, and it squeezes the air **one third of the way from the glottis**, far in the back.
**Dune** is a **high back** vowel that also has **rounding**, with the lips very close together.
**Dan** is a vowel that is **low and front**.

teaching.text: **The vowel /u/ has two constrictions**, one made with the tongue far in the back and one made at the lips.
children: The **constriction at the back has no effect on any of the formants**, even though it is large, because raising mass and stiffness there changes nothing given where it falls in the modes.
So the lip rounding is the part of /u/ that actually changes the formants.

teaching.text: Vowels differ in **where the air is squeezed** in the vocal tract. A **constriction** is a place where the tongue or lips narrow the passage and squeeze the air.
Done has no constriction, so the airflow is unimpeded everywhere.
Dean, a high front vowel, squeezes the air under the roof of the mouth, two thirds of the way from the **glottis**, the tiny space between the vocal folds at the fixed end.

Don, a low back vowel, squeezes the air one third of the way from the glottis, far in the back, while Dune, a high back vowel, also has rounding with the lips very close together, and Dan is low and front.

**/u/ has two constrictions**, one with the tongue far in the back and one at the lips. The constriction at the back has no effect on any of the formants, even though it is large, because of where it falls in the modes.
So the lip rounding is the part of /u/ that actually changes the formants.

sections.title: Why a constriction can raise one formant and lower another

teaching.text: **Constricting air makes it stiffer.** Squeezing air is like pumping up a tire, because the more the air is squeezed, the **stiffer** the tire gets.

**Constricting air also makes it more massive.** Squeezing air into a smaller volume raises its **density**, and **the smaller the volume, the higher the density**, so constricted air is effectively **heavier**.

**So a constriction raises both the effective mass and the effective stiffness.** The false conclusion is that the two cancel, but **they do not**, because speech is full of changing frequencies even though all a speaker does is raise mass and stiffness in different parts of the tract.
children: The real answer comes from **location**. At a point with **no motion but lots of stretching and compression**, the added mass does **nothing** and the added stiffness **raises** the frequency.
At a point with **lots of motion and no compression**, the added mass **lowers** the frequency and the added stiffness does **nothing**.
So whether a formant goes up or down depends on **whether its mode is moving or compressing at the constriction**.

teaching.text: **Constricting air makes it stiffer**, just as squeezing the air in a tire makes the tire stiffer. **Constricting air also makes it more massive**, because squeezing air into a smaller volume raises its density, and the smaller the volume, the higher the density.
So a constriction raises both the effective mass and the effective stiffness of the air.
