sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: This **neural network** simulates a very simple piece of human perception. It takes the **two formants**, F1 and F2, of an isolated vowel and **decides which vowel it is**, and its five possible answers are **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**.
children: The **two input neurons** take F1 and F2 from the environment.
**Three hidden layers** of neurons process those two numbers.
The **five output neurons** give the decision, with one neuron for each vowel.
Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer, so the network is fully connected.

teaching.text: **The weights are the network's knowledge**, and each one is a positive or negative number. A **positive** weight pushes the next neuron up, a **negative** one pushes it down, and the **bigger** the weight, the stronger the push. The weights in the diagram are made up for teaching, and they stay fixed while the network makes a decision.
Learning works by telling the network the right answer.
children: At first **the weights are random**, so the network "doesn't know anything" and its decisions are stupid.
The right answer is given as a **probability distribution**, so for a recording of dean it puts all of the probability on dean, meaning the network should be **completely sure it was dean**.
That target is usually very different from the distribution the stupid network produces at first. The difference is a **mistake**, and the network learns by correcting its mistakes.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries one input through the network to a decision. The example vowel has a **low F1 and a high F2**, and it is one person's /i/.

**Every step is an inner product**, which means multiplying each incoming number by its weight and adding the results, so for the top neuron of the first hidden layer, the inner product is w₁ F1 + w₂ F2
children: Here w1 is the weight from F1, which is small and positive, and w2 is the weight from F2, which is small and negative.
The F1 part adds a little and the F2 part takes away a little more, so this neuron's **activation** lands **just below zero**.
The other neurons do the same thing with their own weights, and layer by layer the activations become the inputs to the next inner products, until the network reaches a decision.
Since the two weights point in opposite directions, **a higher F1 pushes this neuron up and a higher F2 pushes it down**.

teaching.text: **The last numbers are turned into a probability distribution**, a set of numbers that **add up to one**, and the operation that does this is called **softmax**. pᵢ = exp(zᵢ) / (Σⱼ exp(zⱼ))
children: Here zi is one vowel's final score, and pi is its probability.
Softmax makes every score positive and divides each one by the total, so **a bigger score always gives a bigger probability** and all five add up to one.
Raising one vowel's score **lowers the probabilities of the others**, since they all share the same total.

teaching.text: With these weights, **done gets the highest probability, a little over half**, so **the network decides "done."** But the correct answer is **dean**, so the network's knowledge is wrong and it has to change its weights.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Vowel formants overlap across five categories

teaching.text: The vowel data from the class's own lab is plotted with **F1 along one axis and F2 along the other**, with hundreds of recordings and the same number for each vowel. **Each vowel forms a cloud of points**, since the same vowel comes out a little differently every time.
**Some of the patterns are clear.**
children: **The vowel /i/, as in dean**, sits apart with a **high F2 and a low F1**, as the theory predicts.
**The vowel /ae/, as in Dan**, spreads toward **high values of F1**.
So /i/ is clearly different from /u/, the vowel of dune.

teaching.text: **But there is a lot of overlap.**
children: **The vowels of dune, Don and done crowd into the same region**, with a middle F1 and a fairly low F2.
So a new speaker whose formants land in that region could be saying any of the three.

Some points are probably **errors**, but real data always has errors, just as talking to an AI on a train has background noise and a photo in bright sun has glare. Those points stay in the data because **that is what real life is like**.

teaching.text: **This overlap is why AI is hard.** If every vowel sat in its own separate spot, recognizing vowels would be easy, but instead a network has to see the data **many times** to learn what really separates the vowels. **No setting of the weights can separate recordings that land on top of each other**, because two formants are all the network gets.
This overlap was discovered when **Peterson and Barney** measured the vowels of many speakers from spectrograms.
children: They found an **enormous overlap** between vowels and realized that speech recognition would be far harder than anyone expected.

For decades, people tried to write programs to solve it, including trying to **normalize** away the differences between speakers, but **none of it worked**, and what finally worked was **a neural network trained with backpropagation**.

teaching.text: **Static vowels turned out to be harder than moving speech.** For years, everyone predicted that a **static** problem like this one, with two formants from one moment, would be easy, and that **dynamic** speech, with formants always changing, would be very hard. **Everyone turned out to be wrong**, because large language models deal with very dynamic information and work much better, since they use information from before and after each moment.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** is the algorithm that **changes all the weights** so that the network makes better decisions, and it is made of **two algorithms** working together.
children: **Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)** improves each weight **gradually**, in the same way that SGD improved an estimate of an average from data, and it has the same issues, including a **learning rate**.
**Dynamic programming** decides the **order**, so the last weights get improved first, then the ones before them, and so on back to the start.

teaching.text: **Comparing two outputs gives the error.**
children: The **computed output** is what the network produced, which here puts most of the probability on done and only a small amount on dean.
The **desired output** is the right answer, with all of the probability on dean, and a target with a single one and zeros everywhere else is called a **one-hot target**.
The difference between them is the **error**, also called the **loss**. Here the loss depends on how much probability went to dean, so **more probability on dean means less error.**

teaching.text: The error says exactly how each output should move. **The probability of done should go down, the probability of dean should go up, and the probabilities of the other vowels should go down.**
Each weight is changed with the **update rule**. W ← W - η (∂L / ∂W)
children: Here W is a weight and L is the loss, and the fraction tells **whether raising that weight would raise or lower the error**.
The symbol η is the **learning rate**, which is the size of each step.
**The minus sign moves each weight in whichever direction lowers the error.**

teaching.text: **The weights are changed from the end backward**, starting with the connections into the outputs, then the connections into the third hidden layer, then the second, and then the first. The activations from the forward pass stay fixed and are reused.
children: The weight from a positive neuron into **dean gets bigger**, so it adds more to dean.
The weights from the negative neurons into dean **get smaller**, so they take less away from dean.
The weight from that same positive neuron into **done gets smaller**, which lowers the wrong answer.
The weights leaving the formants **barely move**, because they use a much smaller step to match the big values in hertz.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: The same thing has to be asked about every weight, which is **whether the error will go up or down if this weight goes up**. The weights at the **end** of the network are much easier to change than those at the **beginning**.
**The end weights are easy because they directly change the decision.**
children: Done's probability comes partly from multiplying a positive end weight by a positive activation, along with the other products feeding done.
**If that end weight went up, done's probability would go up**, which is the exact opposite of what is needed.
So **that end weight should go down**, and any change to an end weight is **directly, automatically and immediately** reflected in the probabilities.

teaching.text: **The beginning weights are hard because their effect is buried under many layers.**
children: Changing a weight in the first layer changes that layer's **activations**, since activations are inner products of the weights with the inputs.
Those changed activations change the activations of the **next layer**, even with that layer's weights held fixed.
Those changes reach the **third layer**, and the third layer's changes finally reach the **probabilities**.

So **changing an early weight changes one thing, which changes another, which changes another, which finally changes the decision.** Just by looking at it, there is no way to tell which direction it should move, but backpropagation still figures it out.

teaching.text: **This is the same trap as the greedy choice in dynamic programming.** Picking the cheaper of two next steps without looking ahead can lead to the wrong answer, and in the same way, a weight's local appearance says little about its effect on the final decision.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming says that if problems can be ordered by difficulty, the easiest should be solved first, then the next, and so on up to the hardest**, and backpropagation follows exactly that order.
**The last weights, W5, are the easiest problem.**
children: **The output probabilities are directly determined by the last weights**, so **the error is very directly determined by them** as well.
So the error can be used **right away** to decide how to change W5.

teaching.text: **The first weights, W2, are the hardest problem.**
children: **W2 affects its own activations, which then affect another two layers of activations along with many other weights.**
So it is **really hard to figure out how much blame W2 deserves** for a mistake made all the way at the end.
Moreover, **the effect of W2 on the error already includes the effect of W5**, because W5 is downstream of W2.

teaching.text: **Solving the end first makes the rest easier.** Changing the last weights first teaches something that makes the problem of the next layer easier, which makes the layer after it easy too, all the way back to the start, and that is exactly dynamic programming. So **backpropagation is Bellman and Viterbi's dynamic programming combined with SGD**, where SGD improves each weight a little at a time and dynamic programming says to go **from the end backward**.

**Backpropagation is central to the world right now**, because modern AI systems run it on enormous numbers of weights, step by step, for months. These ideas come from **physics** and are closely tied to the **dynamical systems** behind acoustics and masses and springs.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: To train the network, it gets **two matrices**, which are **tables of numbers** with one row for each student recording.
children: The **input matrix, Formant_Inputs**, has two columns, and each row holds one recording's **F1 and F2**.
The **target matrix, TrueVowel_Outputs**, has five columns, and each row is a **one-hot answer**, with a one for the true vowel and a zero for the others, in the order done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.

**Each row in one table goes with the same row in the other**, so a row of the target with all zeros and a one in the Dan column tells the network that it should be completely sure that recording is Dan.
The rows on display are only a sample of the full set of recordings.

teaching.text: **Learning picks rows one at a time.**
children: It takes one row and uses its weights to calculate a decision for that row's formants.
If that decision differs from the desired answer, it **changes its weights**, the last ones first and then back toward the start.
It then picks another row and does the same thing again.

teaching.text: **If the network already gets a row right, there is no error, so there is nothing to learn from that row.** That can be a serious problem, because a network can make the right decision **by accident** over and over and stop learning early, without ever learning the **real pattern** underneath the data.
**Children learning English have the same problem**, as **Carol Chomsky** discovered.
children: At first, very young children say **"go"** and **"went"** correctly, because they are just **memorizing** what they hear.

Then they notice the real pattern, that most English verbs add **-ed** for the past, as in **jump, jumped** and **dance, danced**, and they start saying **"goed."** They have learned the rule, so they make **new mistakes**.
Only later do they learn that **some verbs are exceptions**, and then they get both the regular and the exceptional verbs right.
**Neural networks have the same issue**, because they can just **memorize** weights that give the right answers without learning the pattern, and that is what makes learning so difficult.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: A short **Python program** builds and trains the network. **It never has to be written from scratch**, and the brackets and dots do not matter, because what matters is **what the lines do**.
**The import lines bring in libraries.**
children: A **library** is a collection of programs that one group writes for one job and that others use without knowing how they work inside.
The lines **import torch** and **from torch import nn** **bring into Python everything needed for doing inner products, backpropagation and related work.**
Without libraries, the whole training program could never fit on one page.

teaching.text: The command **torch.load** **loads** the saved tables, the formants and the one-hot answers. Loading means bringing information in, the same thing that happens when a file is double-clicked, and **.float()** makes the values decimal numbers.

**The word Sequential means a neural network that is a sequence of layers.** All the networks built so far are a sequence of layers, while a **large language model** is a network that is **not** just a sequence of layers.

**Each Linear line is one processing layer**, meaning a layer that has weights and does **inner products** with the incoming information. **Linear means just use inner products**, so the formulas never have to be written out.
children: The first layer, **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, says that it receives information from **two** neurons and has **three** neurons of its own.
The next lines take **three and make two**, take **two and make four**, and take **four and make five**.
The network has **five layers but only four lines**, because the **input layer does no processing** and just receives the two formants.
No activation function sits between the layers, so the hidden layers are **linear**.

teaching.text: **The last lines are the only lines PyTorch needs for learning.**
children: The word **SGD** stands for **stochastic gradient descent**, and **lr** stands for the **learning rate**.
**A bigger learning rate learns a lot faster but is less accurate, while a smaller one is more accurate but learns much more slowly.**
The **loss** is **the mistake**, since the network calculates its mistakes and learns from them, and **CrossEntropyLoss** takes the raw scores and handles the probability part itself.
The command **zero_grad()** clears the old corrections, **backward()** is **backpropagation**, and **step()** changes the weights.
**Computing the corrections and changing the weights are separate steps**, so nothing changes until step() runs, and here all of the rows go through together for **one full step**.

teaching.text: The program starts from **PyTorch's own default weights and biases**, not the hand-picked weights in the diagram, so the structure matches but the numbers would not.

A short **Python program** builds and trains the network, and it never has to be written from scratch, since brackets and dots do not matter. **The import lines bring in libraries**, collections of programs that other people wrote for one job, which can be used without knowing how they work inside.
Before libraries like PyTorch existed, everyone doing AI had to write their own backpropagation code.
The import lines import into Python everything for doing inner products, backpropagation and related work, which is why the whole training program fits on one page.

**Sequential means a neural network that is a sequence of layers.** All the networks built so far are a sequence of layers, while a large language model is a network that is not just a sequence of layers. **Each Linear line is one processing layer**, a layer that has weights and does inner products with the incoming information.
The first linear line says it receives information from two neurons and has three neurons, and the following lines go from three to two, two to four, and four to five.
The network has five layers but only four lines, because the input layer does no processing.

**The last lines are the only lines PyTorch needs for learning.** SGD is stochastic gradient descent and lr is the learning rate, here 0.1. **A bigger learning rate learns a lot faster but is less accurate, while a smaller one is more accurate but learns much slower.**
Loss is the mistake, so the network calculates its mistakes and learns from them, and backward is backpropagation.
Nothing changes until step is called, which is when the weights actually change.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: **Neural networks do not come out of nowhere**, because their basic features come from **discoveries about animal brains**. Scientists found that brains have **neurons**, so networks have neurons, and they found that **each neuron collects information from many other neurons**, which is the **inner product**.

**Adrian** discovered that **neurons are nearly digital, because they either fire or they do not fire.** A real neuron's activation is not some in-between number, because it is basically **off or on**, while the neurons of the vowel network can take any value at all.

**The sigmoid** is an **activation function** that was added to networks to copy Adrian's discovery. It takes a neuron's **linear activation**, which is its inner product, and turns it into a number **between zero and one**. σ(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
children: Here z is the inner product, and σ(z) is the new activation.
**If the inner product is large and positive, the sigmoid is near one, and if it is large and negative, the sigmoid is basically zero.**

So a fairly negative inner product and a hugely negative one both come out near zero, a fairly positive one and a hugely positive one both come out near one, and only inner products close to zero land in between.
In this way **the sigmoid digitizes neural processing**, copying the brain chemistry that keeps real neurons close to off or on.

teaching.text: **The S shape changes how differences come out.** Near zero the curve is **steep**, so a small change in the inner product makes a big change in the output, while far from zero it is **flat**, so even big changes barely matter. **Animal perception reflects this, because some things that seem alike are perceived as different and some things that are very different are perceived as the same.**

**AI is duplicating the abilities of animals.** Engineers build in what biologists discover and then add their own ideas, so they might replace the sigmoid with other functions of a similar shape, such as **ReLU**. **People will say that AI has nothing to do with human cognition, but that is false**, because a big reason it works is that it copies our own abilities, using math as simple as multiplying and adding.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: The sigmoid is added **one hidden neuron at a time**, while the input and every weight stay the same. The neurons switch in layer order, first the ones in the first hidden layer, then the second, then the third, and the outputs still use softmax.

The first neuron to switch has an inner product **just below zero**, which sits on the steep middle of the curve, so it comes out **just under one half**. The neuron now sends a **positive** number instead of a negative one.

**After each switch, everything downstream is recalculated**, because later neurons depend on earlier ones. So the sigmoid network cannot be made by running the old linear numbers through the sigmoid one at a time, since each new value has to come from the updated layer before it.

With **every hidden neuron on sigmoid**, every hidden activation sits between zero and one, and the answer moves completely. **Dan becomes the top answer**, **dean rises to second place**, and **done drops well behind**. **Only the activation rule changed and no weight moved, so this is not learning**, and even though the decision changed completely, **dean is still not the top answer**.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The command **nn.Sigmoid()** is added after each of the first three Linear layers. **The command nn.Sigmoid means apply the sigmoid, which makes the neurons digital**, and the layer sizes stay exactly the same, because the sigmoid changes values but not how many there are.

**The last layer, nn.Linear(4, 5), has no sigmoid**, because its five scores go to the loss, which turns them into probabilities. The **sigmoid** squeezes **each hidden neuron on its own**, while the **softmax** turns **all five final scores together** into a decision that adds up to one.
The training lines and the learning rate stay the same. The program starts from PyTorch's default weights, so it would not reproduce the diagram's exact numbers.

sections.title: One initialization · training the linear network for 2,000 updates

teaching.text: Training runs **thousands of times**, which is far more than the few dozen steps needed to average a list of numbers, and **each full pass of learning is called an epoch.**
children: The starting weights are **random**, and that particular random set is called the **initialization**.
The network is linear, with no biases, and the formants are scaled down from hertz to kilohertz to keep the numbers small.

After every epoch, accuracy is measured without training. **The vowel with the largest score is the network's answer, and accuracy is the percentage of recordings it gets right**, and since these are the same recordings it learns from, this is called **training accuracy**.

teaching.text: **Accuracy starts at twenty percent, which is chance.**
children: At the start the weights are random, so the network knows nothing.
It still is not at zero, because with **five vowels**, a random guess is right **one time in five**.
The word **chance** means how often someone would be right just by guessing randomly, so **with five possible answers, chance is twenty percent.**

teaching.text: **After a couple hundred epochs, accuracy jumps up well above chance**, so the network is **learning something**. It dips back toward chance for a moment, recovers, and then levels off a little below half after a few hundred epochs.

sections.title: Ten initializations · different paths, the same final accuracy

teaching.text: The same training is run **ten times**, each time starting from **different random weights**, while everything else stays identical.
**The runs take different paths but end in the same place.**
children: All ten runs start near **twenty percent**, the level of chance.
Some leave chance quickly and others stay flat longer, and several briefly drop back toward chance.
After a few hundred epochs they **come together**, and **all ten finish at the same accuracy, a little below half**.
So **different starting weights change the path but not the destination**, because the learning process is so similar each time.

teaching.text: **The network levels off well below perfect accuracy because the data overlap so much.** Its final accuracy is clearly better than chance, so the network has learned something, but it is still pretty low.
children: **AI is not some kind of magic.** If a person had to name the vowel for formants landing where several vowels overlap, they would have to squint hard and might still guess wrong.
**If the decision is very hard for humans, it is not surprising that it is hard for machines.**
The limit comes from **two formants not being enough to separate dune, Don and done**, not from unlucky starting weights, so trying more starting points would not help.

teaching.text: **Different network designs can be tested in lab** by adding or removing layers, changing the number of neurons, or swapping in the sigmoid or other functions, and each change is checked for whether it **improves** that accuracy or makes it worse.

sections.title: NNs → LLMs → Agentic Systems
Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories

teaching.text: A **neural network** takes in information about **one moment**, uses its **weights** to process it, and makes a **decision**, and it learns those weights by **making errors and correcting them through backpropagation**. The vowel network is this kind of system, because it takes **two formants**, passes them through **three hidden layers**, and decides among **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**.
**The idea began with a paper by McCulloch and Pitts**, which proposed that simple mathematics could model how the brain works, and that paper described the first artificial neural network.
children: The paper starts from the **"all-or-none"** character of nervous activity, where **"all" means active and "none" means inactive**, so a neuron is either firing or not firing.

That is the same idea as the **sigmoid**, which pushes a neuron's activation toward off or on, so **the very first paper on artificial neural networks starts from biology about how real neurons behave.**
The earliest work on neural networks was about modeling how the human mind works, not about making money.

teaching.text: Later, the ideas matured into the two **Parallel Distributed Processing** books.
children: The word **parallel** means that many neurons compute their activations **at the same time**, so all of the neurons in one layer work together, then all of the neurons in the next layer, and so on.
The word **distributed** means that the information from F1 and F2 is **spread across all of the neurons** instead of sitting in any one of them.
By then, **forward propagation and backpropagation** were well worked out.

teaching.text: **Given some static vector of formants, these networks could make a decision about a few possible categories.** A **vector** is just a list of numbers, and **static** means one fixed list from one moment.
What these networks lacked is that **human cognition is far more complex** than taking in one list of numbers and giving one decision at the end.
children: **Speech is incredibly time-varying**, because speakers do not produce one F1 and one F2, and **every little moment in time gives a new formant.**
**Language is time-varying too**, because a sentence is a whole bunch of words, one after another, and answering a question about it uses all of them.
So **giving a network one bunch of numbers can never model cognition that unfolds in time**, and many researchers were aware of this.

sections.title: Jordan’s recurrent network for speech production

teaching.text: **Michael Jordan** developed **recurrent neural networks** to make sense of **speech production**, which is how the tongue, velum and lips move over time.
children: He studied features such as **nasality**, which depends on the velum going up and down, and **rounding**, which depends on the lips.
He realized that **a regular neural network could never handle something that complex and time-varying**.

So he designed a new kind of network, and that line of work **became large language models and then agentic AI**, which means that the technology at the center of modern AI was born from thinking about **speech**.

teaching.text: **His network is not just sequential.** In a PyTorch network, **Sequential** means one layer after another, while Jordan's network has **two layers working in parallel**, a kind of network he invented for speech production.
children: The **plan units** take outside input and say what sequence to produce.
The **hidden units** combine information, and the **output units** give the response.
The **state units** are the new part, because they hold what the network has **just produced**.

teaching.text: **The network is called recurrent because it takes its output and sends it back into part of its input.**
children: The network produces something at **one moment**, and that output loops back into the **state units**, which also feed back into themselves.
The network then uses it to predict the **next moment**, and uses that to predict the moment after, and so on.

The details of how recurrent networks work do not need to be learned, because what matters is that **cognition, and speech production especially, means understanding a whole unfolding of events in time**.

teaching.text: In the network's **performance on a sequence of speech sounds**, each row is an articulatory feature, such as voicing, nasality, tongue height and rounding. The feature for **rounding rises early and stays high across many sounds**, because the outputs fed back from one moment carry into the next.
**GPT works the same way, one word at a time.**
children: A prompt goes in, and the system predicts **the next word**, which is the first word of its answer.
It then feeds the prompt **plus that word** back in and predicts the next word again.
It keeps feeding everything back in and predicting, and people kept refining recurrent networks along these lines until **large language models** were invented.

teaching.text: **Science and technology evolve from other people's ideas over long stretches of time**, as early ideas about neurons were refined into later networks and Jordan's idea was refined into large language models. The people who came up with these ideas were mostly not the ones who made a lot of money from them.

sections.title: From one neuron to agentic systems

teaching.text: AI systems build up in steps, and **each step extends the one before it**.
**A single neuron takes in a list of numbers and gives back one number.**
children: A neuron takes information from all of the neurons feeding it, multiplies each input **x** by its weight **w**, and **adds them all up**, which is the **inner product**.
The symbol **Σ**, called sigma, just means **add them all up**.

This uses nothing but second-grade multiplication and addition to model the electrochemical activity of a real neuron, so **a profound idea that moves science and society can start out incredibly simple.**

teaching.text: **A neural network takes in one list of numbers and gives back a whole list of decisions.**
children: Its layers of neurons are linked by sets of weights, labeled **W₁, W₂ and W₃**.
**Each set of weights turns one list of numbers into the next** through many inner products.
The last layer is a **decision vector**, with one value for each possible answer.
This is the kind of network that was built for the vowels, and it still takes only **one list of numbers**.

teaching.text: **A large language model takes in many lists of numbers, one for each moment in a sequence, and gives back one decision about what comes next.**
children: It takes **a whole bunch of vectors**, here fifteen of them, and **each vector stands for something happening at one moment in time**, such as **one word** of a sentence.
In real systems the vectors number in the **hundreds of thousands to a million**, and that set is called the **context window**. Each vector is also **thousands of numbers long**.

The job is to **predict the sixteenth vector**, which is **a probability distribution over the next word**, with one entry for every word in the vocabulary giving the likelihood that each word comes next.

teaching.text: **A large language model is made of neural networks.** Each block of **W's** is a **layer**, which is a neural network in its own right, and real systems have **hundreds of layers**. **The knowledge is still in the W's**, just as in a single network, so if an LLM writes an essay, its knowledge of how to write one is stored in its weights.
**A large language model is also a dynamical system**, and that is why the Nobel Prize for AI was awarded in **physics**.
children: A mass-spring system is a **dynamical system**, because it starts from **initial conditions**, such as where the mass starts and how fast it is moving, and then the system itself decides what happens over time.

An LLM works the same way, because **its initial condition is the set of input vectors.** Each layer uses its W's to turn those vectors into **better vectors**, and then better ones again, sometimes hundreds of times, until by the last layer the vectors are good enough to **predict the next word**.
The mass-spring system had only **two numbers** to keep track of, while an LLM has **thousands** in each vector, but it is the same idea.

teaching.text: **The calculation at every step is the inner product**, so the whole system just multiplies and adds, billions or trillions of times.
**A large language model learns by predicting the next word and correcting its mistakes.**
children: A sentence such as **"The cat sat on the"** goes in, and the real next word is **"mat."**
At first the **W's are random**, so the model predicts something stupid, such as **"in,"** which is impossible, since "the" cannot be followed by "in."
**Backpropagation** then adjusts all of its weights so that the prediction moves closer to "mat."

This is repeated with an enormous number of sentences, and **surprisingly, the system ends up knowing how to speak English.** Nobody who studied human thought would have believed that plain inner products, plus the sigmoid or functions like it, could do human language, but it works.

teaching.text: **The first problem large language models solved was machine translation**, such as turning a text in English into French. People then tried the same design on speech and many other problems, and **it worked for all kinds of things.**

**Closure is a principle from Gestalt psychology.** In the figure of three broken circles, people see a whole triangle even though no triangle is drawn, because the mind fills in what is missing. The cloze procedure applies the same principle to language. It was invented as a way of measuring how readable a piece of writing is, by deleting words and asking readers to fill them in. Given "chickens cackle and blank quack", almost anyone fills in ducks right away. Filling that gap correctly requires knowing the meanings of the words, how they combine, and the structure of the whole sentence.

**An agentic system is a graph of large language models**, with several of them passing their output to one another, and **an agent in AI today is just an LLM.** Today's chat and programming systems work this way.
**Each LLM in the graph gets one job.**
children: The first LLM gets the prompt with the instruction **not to write the answer but to outline it**, and that is how these systems produce long, well-structured answers.
The next LLM takes the outline and writes it out in **smooth sentences**.
Another LLM has the job of a **critic**, and its only job is to **criticize** the draft.

A revision LLM decides whether the draft is good enough, and if it is not, it sends the draft **back to the critic**, so there is a **loop between the critic and the reviser** that usually runs for a few rounds.
The last LLM produces the final output.

teaching.text: **The critic is what fixed hallucination.**
children: When systems only outlined and then wrote, **hallucination**, which is the system making things up, was a huge problem.
Adding an LLM whose **only job is to criticize** the writer's draft is the reason there is much less hallucination now.
This back-and-forth is why many systems take a while to respond, and the text that sometimes flies by is the **LLMs talking to each other**.

teaching.text: **The levels build up like a body.** Molecules make cells, cells make organs, and organs make a body, and in the same way **neurons make neural networks, neural networks make LLMs, and LLMs make agentic systems**, with each level inheriting the abilities of the level below it.

**Designing these graphs is a real job**, and it does not require knowing many programming languages. Instead it requires **problem solving**, which means taking a problem in the world and **designing a graph of LLMs that will solve it**.
**The chief insight behind all of this is Gestalt completion.**
children: In the Gestalt figure, people **see a triangle even though no triangle is drawn**, because they put the pieces together and complete it.
Gestalt psychologists knew long ago that **completion is a very important part of human knowledge**.

So **training a system only to predict the missing thing turns out to emulate human cognition.** No one would have believed that this would work, or that it would use only inner products, sigmoids and a few other simple operations.

teaching.text: **Two operations run underneath everything, from one neuron all the way up to an agentic system.**
children: **Inference is inner products**, because every decision is made by multiplying and adding.
**Learning is SGD plus dynamic programming**, which together make backpropagation.

sections.title: Fifteen vectors · the same next-item question for any sequence

teaching.text: **A large language model takes fifteen vectors, x₁ through x₁₅, and predicts x₁₆.** A vector is just a list of numbers, so **those numbers can stand for almost anything**, and whatever they stand for, the machine plays the same game of **predicting the next one**.

The vectors can be **words**, with each vector standing for **one word** of a sentence, such as **"The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the ___,"** where **x₁₆ is the missing next word.**
children: A speaker of English knows a likely completion, such as **"branch"** or **"mat."**
A new LLM starts with random W's and predicts something silly, and **backpropagation on all of its weights** moves its prediction toward a sensible word.
Getting it right means using **the whole sentence**, since it was **the cat**, not the dog, that sat.

teaching.text: The vectors can be **slices of sound**, because the same system was applied to **spectrograms**.
children: A spectrogram is cut into **little frames**, each frame becomes one vector of **frequencies and amplitudes**, and **x₁₆ is the next frame.**
So the system learns to **predict the next little piece of speech from all of the previous pieces**.
The result was **the best speech recognition ever built**, and it is also the basis for **speech synthesis** that is now very hard to tell from a human voice.

teaching.text: The vectors can be **pieces of a picture**, because the same thing was done with **images**.
children: A picture is cut into **sixteen patches** read row by row, each patch becomes a vector of pixel values, and **x₁₆ is the missing bottom-right patch.**
Trained to **predict the missing piece** across huge numbers of pictures, the system learns what a dog, a dolphin or a boat is.
This became the basis of modern **computer vision** and image classifiers.

teaching.text: The vectors can even be **molecules**, because the same idea was applied to **proteins**.
children: A **protein** is a string of **amino acids**, which come in twenty kinds, each written as one letter, and proteins make up hair, teeth, blood and nearly everything else in the body.
The **insulin B chain** is read as fifteen amino acids, and **x₁₆ is the next one**.

One of the hardest problems in science is **protein folding**, which is how a chain of amino acids folds into its particular shape, and solving folding leads to better **drug design** and **vaccines**.
Treating a protein as **just a sequence of amino acids** and playing the same game of predicting the next one pushed the folding problem many years ahead.

teaching.text: **The large language model only ever sees vectors.** Words, sounds, pixels and molecules all reach it the same way, so one machine asks one question, which is what x₁₆ will be, and it does so **with the same architecture every time**.

**Prediction from the past has limits.** These systems predict the next thing from **past data**, so when something new happens that the past data does not cover, they can **hallucinate**, and some systems are now told to say "I don't know" instead of guessing.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: English allows only **certain sequences of sounds** in its words, and knowing which sequences are allowed is called **phonotactic knowledge**.
**A simple syllable in English can have a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, which is written **CVC**, and words like **Don, mat, sit, cup, dog, fish, ring and van** follow this pattern.
children: The pattern is about **sounds, not letters**, so the **silent e** in **shave, kite and rope** does not count.
Two letters can also spell one consonant sound, as in **ship, chin and bath**.

teaching.text: **Syllables can also have clusters**, which are groups of consonants together. A cluster **before the vowel** is called an **onset**, and a cluster **after the vowel** is called a **coda**.
children: Real onset clusters appear in **split, flat, black, glad and stop**, and real coda clusters appear in **desk, box, help, milk and lamp**.
Each real word has an **impossible twin**, marked with a star. The onset twins are ***sblit, *lfat, *bnack, *dlad and *tsop**, and the coda twins are ***desb, *bokp, *hepl, *mikl and *lapm**.
Many twins use **the same letters in the other order**, such as **flat and *lfat**, **help and *hepl**, and **lamp and *lapm**, so **the order of the sounds matters**.

**The order mirrors around the vowel.** In **flat**, the **l sits right next to the vowel** and the f is farther out, and in **help**, the **l again sits next to the vowel**, now on the other side, with the p farther out. In **lamp**, the **m sits next to the vowel**, and each impossible twin puts the wrong consonant against the vowel.
So **only certain sequences are allowed before the vowel and after the vowel.**

teaching.text: **A long word is a chain of syllables**, marked with dots at the breaks, as in **ba·na·na, At·lan·tic, ath·lete and ad·mit**.
children: **The sounds t and l are fine across a syllable break, but tl cannot start a syllable**, which is why **Atlantic** is a word but ***tlantic** is impossible, and why **athlete** and **admit** work but ***thlete** and ***dmit** do not.
The sound **ng** can end a syllable, as in **ring**, but it can **never start one**, so ***ngapkin** is impossible.
Starting a word with a bad cluster, as in ***bnanana** or ***sbaghetti**, breaks the rules even when the rest of the word is fine.
So **whether a sequence is allowed depends on where the syllable breaks fall.**

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: **Phonotactic knowledge can be revealed through GPT learning.** Each item is **the start of an English word**, and the task is to **guess the next letter**. People **agree on their guesses quickly**, and **how much they agree changes from item to item**.

**Almost anything can follow once a vowel has come.** After **ra_**, likely letters include **t, n, r and l**, and many others are possible too, because the onset is over once the vowel arrives, so the guesses **spread out**.
**At the start of a word, the choices narrow sharply** to exactly what an English onset allows.
children: After **sp_**, the next letter is **l, r or a vowel**, and **never n**, so *spn is impossible.
After **k_**, the next letter is **a vowel or n**, as in **knee**, and **never t**, so *kt is impossible.
After **b_** and **f_**, the next letter is **r, l or a vowel**, and **never n**, so *bn and *fn are impossible.
After **sh_**, the next letter is **a vowel or r**, as in **shrimp**, and **never b**, so *shb is impossible.
After **skr_** or after **m_** at the start of a word, **only a vowel** can come, so *skrl and *mb are impossible.
After **bram_**, the letter **b** is almost forced, as in **bramble**, though **a new syllable** could also start there.

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter is the same as predicting x₁₆.** The letters so far are the sequence, and the next letter is the thing to predict, which is the same **game of predicting the next token** that an LLM plays.
children: **A GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling**, because its predictions can only get good by matching the patterns of English syllables.
Its prediction is a **probability distribution** over the next letter, and **the shape of that distribution carries the knowledge**.
After **fa_**, the distribution is **flat**, spread over many letters, since almost anything can follow a vowel.
After **skr_**, the distribution is **sharply peaked** on a few vowels, since English allows nothing else there.
So **the more the letters so far restrict what can come next, the more the probability piles onto a few letters.**

lecture18.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate

teaching.text: **A neuron takes a list of inputs and combines them into one response.** Each incoming number is multiplied by its weight, and the products are added together. This **inner product** is a simple mathematical model of how inputs from other neurons contribute to a neuron's activity.
children: A **vector** is a list of numbers, so one vector supplies the inputs and one number gives the response.
The **weights** decide how strongly the inputs contribute. A larger contribution changes the response more strongly, so changing the weights changes what the system does with its input.

Multiplication and addition are elementary operations, but repeating them across many connected units creates a system with much more complex behavior. Complexity grows through the organization of simple parts.

teaching.text: **A neural network combines many neurons into a decision-making system.** Every neuron in one layer produces a response, and those responses become the list of inputs received by the following layer.
children: The small network has layers of **four, three, four and five units**, linked by weight sets **W₁, W₂ and W₃**. Each set changes one list of numbers into another.

The final list is a **decision vector**, with a response for each possible answer. The vowel recognizer uses formants to decide which vowel was spoken, so a fixed list of measurements becomes a category decision.

A decision based on one fixed list captures only one part of cognition. Speech and language unfold through sequences, and understanding a sequence depends on keeping information from earlier parts available.

teaching.text: **A large language model processes many vectors and predicts the following item.** In the example, fifteen input vectors pass through five layers, and the output is a prediction about the sixteenth item.
children: A **token** is an item in the sequence that the model processes or predicts. In a word example, each input vector represents a word already supplied, while the output gives probabilities for possible next words.

A **probability distribution** expresses which continuations are more likely. Its probabilities add up to one, so assigning more probability to one answer leaves less probability for the other possibilities.

The weights contain learned information that allows the system to make this prediction. Each layer changes the representations received from the layer before it, until the resulting vectors support a useful next-token decision.

teaching.text: **Knowing a language allows a person to predict a continuation from relationships that may stretch across many words.** A sentence beginning with **the dog** can contain intervening material about **my parents**, people who live far away, and other singular or plural things, before reaching the verb about the dog.
children: The suitable continuation is **barks**, because the verb belongs with the singular **dog**. If the subject were **dogs**, the corresponding continuation would be **bark**.

The nearest noun is therefore not enough to decide the answer. Information about the dog must remain available while the intervening words are processed, because those words do not change which noun the verb belongs with.

**Syntax** concerns how words are organized into sentences. Learning syntax includes learning dependencies between words, rather than learning only which word tends to occur immediately beside another.

teaching.text: **An LLM learns to make a prediction by changing its weights when its answer is wrong.** A training sentence supplies both the sequence so far and the actual following word, allowing the prediction to be compared with the target.
children: If the model predicts an unsuitable word instead of **barks**, the error is used to change weights throughout its layers and heads. The changes should make the appropriate continuation more likely when the same kind of context occurs again.

**Backpropagation works backward from the output**, using the effects already calculated for later connections to work out the effects of earlier ones. Reusing those answers is **dynamic programming**, and **stochastic gradient descent** uses the error information to adjust the weights.

**Inference uses learned weights to process an input, while learning changes those weights.** Improving a prediction during training and producing an answer with the current weights are different operations.

teaching.text: **Multilingual systems learn patterns from more than one language.** Learning how words go together in English and Dutch concerns related languages, while learning Japanese or Navajo involves languages with very different structures.
children: Their common problem is still predicting and organizing sequences. A multilingual system can use learned patterns across languages, while the details of the permitted word orders differ.

The same system can respond in different human languages instead of requiring a separate program for every language. A language model can also learn programming and database languages, because their symbols occur in structured sequences too.

teaching.text: **Multimodal systems connect more than one kind of information.** Text, speech and pictures are different **modalities**, and a system can learn correspondences between them.
children: Giving a picture and receiving a caption connects visual information with language. Speech recognition connects sound with text, while speech synthesis connects text with sound.

The model has to represent the information in a form it can process and learn the relevant relationships. Using vectors provides a common numerical form without making pictures, sounds and words identical kinds of information.

teaching.text: **An agentic system connects whole LLMs into a graph, giving different models different jobs.** The graph organizes how their responses move between them, instead of using just one uninterrupted pass from the beginning of an answer to its end.
children: An **Outline model** plans the structure of a response, and a **Write model** turns that plan into connected prose. Planning first helps organize what the response will contain before its details are filled in.
A **Critic model** evaluates the draft, including whether its statements fit together. A **Revise model** changes it, and the revision can return to the critic for another evaluation.
The **critic and reviser form a loop**, while a **Final model** produces the final response. A controller can coordinate the exchange by deciding which model receives information from another.

teaching.text: **The models communicate through language.** An instruction such as writing from an outline gives another model a job, just as a person can use English to specify what a collaborator should do.
children: The models can also use computer and database languages. A system can combine an English instruction with the ability to produce a program or retrieve structured information.

A language-teaching system with little text available can use these abilities together, organizing the available language information into material for a learner. Building a teacher involves choosing useful material and responding patiently, rather than only predicting words from a large text collection.

teaching.text: **Revising a response is different from retraining the models that produce it.** In the basic agent arrangement, the individual LLMs have already been trained, and their weights stay fixed while they exchange drafts and instructions.
children: The critic's response can change what the reviser writes without changing either model's weights. The loop changes the information being exchanged and the response being produced.

An individual model uses the sequence already supplied as context for its next prediction. An agentic system can also use **shared memory**, a place where agents write and retrieve information, allowing information to remain available across their interactions.
Shared memory and the arrangement of the graph affect how the agents coordinate. These are features of the larger system, while a head is one component inside a layer of an individual LLM.

sections.title: Parallel heads and successive layers

teaching.text: **Predicting the next word is difficult because the needed information can be spread throughout the sequence.** A language model develops its **representations**, the information carried in its vectors, through many successive layers.
children: A later layer receives vectors already changed by the processing before it. Improving a representation means changing it in a way that helps the final prediction, rather than merely making its numerical values larger.

The **architecture** specifies how layers and heads are arranged, while training determines the weights. Choosing the architecture does not by itself reveal every language pattern that these learned weight combinations represent.

teaching.text: **A head is a processing component that contributes to improving a representation.** Several heads work in parallel inside one layer, and their contributions are brought together before the vectors move onward.
children: Imagine asking several experts for advice on how to improve something. Each expert contributes an opinion, and combining those opinions produces an improved result.

The **experts are like heads**, while the **group is like a layer**. A second group adds another stage of improvement, combining new contributions to improve the result received from the preceding group.

The heads are described as experts because each has learned weights that contribute to processing the information. They are components within a model, rather than separate people or whole language models.

teaching.text: **Attention heads consult the sequence to work out which relationships matter for the prediction.** To choose **barks**, the processing must connect the verb with **dog**, despite the intervening words about the parents.
children: Information elsewhere in the sequence can therefore matter more than the word immediately before the prediction. Consulting the sequence makes it possible to use the relevant dependency.

**Heads contribute in parallel within one layer, while layers supply successive stages.** The contributions within a stage are combined, then the next stage works on the representations that combination produced.
**For exam preparation, focus on heads and how their contributions combine within a layer.** Understanding this organization means explaining how it helps produce a useful next-token prediction.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth

teaching.text: **A dynamical system uses a rule to turn its current state into a new state, then applies the rule again to the result.** The **state** is the set of values describing the system at a particular stage, and the starting values are its **initial conditions**.
children: The oscillator begins with **position one and velocity zero**. Because the first position update uses the old velocity, position initially stays unchanged.
The velocity update uses the newly calculated position. That position is positive, so velocity becomes negative, and the following position update then carries the position downward.
Repeatedly applying the rule develops the motion from its starting state. Predicting the future means finding the next state from the current one, then using that result again.

teaching.text: **Position and velocity are updated in an alternating order.** The new position uses the old velocity, and the new velocity uses the new position, so the calculations are **interleaved**.
children: Velocity contributes to how position changes. Positive velocity raises position, while negative velocity lowers it.
Position contributes to how velocity changes, with positive position pushing velocity downward and negative position pushing it upward. This pulls the motion back toward the center.
The sequence of values forms a **trajectory**. Position follows a cosine-like pattern and velocity a shifted, minus-sine-like pattern, while the step size controls how far each update advances.

teaching.text: **A recurrent neural network combines a network with feedback through time.** Jordan's network has **plan units** and **state units** feeding a hidden layer, which produces an output that is copied back into the state units.
children: The state units also have self-connections that retain a fading trace of the earlier state. The next output therefore depends on recent history as well as on the plan input.
The same weights are reused at successive moments. Feeding output back into input allows a repeated rule to generate a developing sequence rather than a single isolated response.

teaching.text: **A language model’s depth plays the role of time in this comparison.** The initial information is the set of input vectors, and each layer transforms the representations produced by the preceding layer.
children: Following one numerical value through the layers gives a changing path, while following many values gives many trajectories. Their curves are not required to be the oscillator's cosine.

The oscillator and recurrent network reuse the same rule across time, while each LLM layer has its own weights. What connects the examples is the dependence of a new state on the state produced before it.

The stock-return sequences also rise and fall over time along different paths. A dynamical description concerns how quantities develop, rather than requiring every changing system to follow one exact oscillation.

Feedback also occurs at the level of the agentic graph when a revised response returns to the critic. The idea of a developing state can therefore connect operations within a model with interactions between models.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences

teaching.text: **Fifteen vectors can represent fifteen words, sound frames, picture patches or amino acids.** In each case the model receives **x₁ through x₁₅** and predicts the following item, **x₁₆**.
children: The words **“The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the ___”** form one sequence. The cat is the one that ran and sat, so a sensible next word depends on the sentence's relationships as well as on nearby words.

A **spectrogram** represents frequencies over time. Its fifteen successive frames supply pieces of a sound, and the prediction is the following frame, with the original frequency range running from zero to five kilohertz.

A picture of a house, a tree and the sun is divided into a **four-by-four arrangement of sixteen patches**. Reading row by row gives an order, with fifteen patches supplied and the missing sixteenth patch at the bottom-right corner.
The **insulin B-chain** example supplies **F V N Q H L C G S H L V E A L**, fifteen amino acids in an ordered chain. The following residue to be predicted is **Y**.

teaching.text: **The numerical form is shared, while what the numbers represent differs.** Sound frames follow time, picture patches follow a chosen reading order through space, and amino acids follow positions along a chain.
children: The folded protein and its written sequence concern the same protein, but the predicted item here is the next amino acid. The example is about continuing an ordered sequence, rather than predicting the entire folded structure.

The model must have suitable representations and learning for the kind of information it processes. Calling each item a vector explains the shared input form without making the original materials interchangeable.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: **Phonotactics is knowledge of which sequences of sounds a language allows.** English speakers can judge whether a possible word fits English patterns without having been explicitly taught every permitted sequence.
children: A simple syllable can have a **consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, as in **Don, mat, sit, fish and ring**. The pattern concerns sounds, so the silent e in **shave, kite and rope** does not add a spoken vowel.
Two letters can spell one consonant sound, as in **ship, chin and bath**. Sound structure and written letter structure therefore have to be distinguished.

teaching.text: **Languages differ in which consonants they allow at the ends of syllables.** The Mandarin comparison focuses on nasal endings, while Cantonese also permits a final **p**, the ending that makes **cup** possible in that comparison.
children: A consonant-vowel-consonant arrangement is therefore not a complete rule for every language. Knowing that three sound positions are present does not determine which consonants a language permits in them.
The permitted sequences form part of a person's language knowledge. A sequence that sounds impossible in one language can fit the structure of another.

teaching.text: **English allows consonant clusters whose order matters.** Clusters before the vowel occur in **split, flat, black, glad and stop**, while clusters after it occur in **desk, box, help, milk and lamp**.
children: A star marks a form unavailable in the English comparison. The onset alternatives are ***sblit, *lfat, *bnack, *dlad and *tsop**, while the coda alternatives are ***desb, *bokp, *hepl, *mikl and *lapm**. Several contain familiar consonants but arrange them in an impermissible order.

In **flat**, the l is next to the vowel with the f farther out. In **help**, the l is again next to the vowel, now on the other side, with the p farther out, so the order mirrors around the vowel in these examples. In **lamp**, m sits next to the vowel and p sits farther out, while ***lapm** reverses that order.

A sequence excluded from English can be possible elsewhere. Russian examples permit initial clusters such as **zb** or **dl**, while the Spanish comparison changes an initial **s followed by a consonant** by placing a vowel before it, as in the comparison with English **stadium**.

teaching.text: **A long word is a chain of syllables, and a boundary changes which sequences are possible.** In **At·lan·tic**, t and l occur across a syllable boundary, while ***tlantic** would place tl together at the beginning.
children: The same kind of contrast separates **athlete** from ***thlete**, and **admit** from ***dmit**. The sound **ng** can finish a syllable, as in **ring**, while ***ngapkin** places it at the beginning in the English contrast.

Forms such as ***bnanana** and ***sbaghetti** begin with clusters unavailable in these English patterns. Familiar later syllables do not make the whole word fit, because the opening still has to follow the language's rules.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: **Predicting a word's next letter uses knowledge of its possible sound and spelling patterns.** After **ra_**, letters such as **t, n, r and l** can follow, while other beginnings allow fewer continuations.
children: After **sp_**, the possibilities include **l, r or a vowel**, while ***spn** does not fit the English pattern. After **b_** or **f_**, r, l or a vowel can follow, while ***bn** and ***fn** do not fit these word beginnings.
After **k_**, a vowel or **n** can follow, as in **knee**, where the written k is silent. After **sh_**, a vowel or r can follow, as in **shrimp**, while ***shb** does not fit.

After **skr_** or initial **m_**, a vowel follows in these patterns, while ***skrl** and ***mb** do not fit. After **bram_**, the expected b gives **bramble**, although a new syllable could also begin there.

teaching.text: **A next-item predictor can learn these regularities by trying to continue the sequences in its training data.** Its probabilities express how strongly the context supports different following items.
children: A relatively open beginning permits probability to be spread over many continuations, while a restricted beginning concentrates the suitable choices. The contrast between **ra_ and skr_** connects prediction with knowledge of possible English sequences.

Learning syllable structure gives a smaller problem than learning how all the words of a language form sentences. The sound inventory is limited, but the permitted combinations still have to be learned.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables

teaching.text: **A model designed to learn English word patterns uses four attention heads in each of five layers and sixty-four numbers in each token vector.** These are architecture choices, with the heads contributing within layers and the layers supplying successive transformations.
children: The initial training design uses **one thousand randomly chosen English words**. For each word, the model is intended to predict the next letter from the letters already supplied and change the weights after an error.

The design calls for **ten generated examples after each training step**, allowing the developing output to be inspected. The generated examples are a way to examine what the model currently produces, rather than proof by themselves that it has learned English.

A **pronunciation lexicon** supplies information about how words sound, allowing training to focus on pronunciation rather than treating every written letter as a separate sound. This matters for forms such as **shave**, whose final e is not separately pronounced.

teaching.text: **An initial run of this model still produced largely gibberish.** Some forms may have contained vowels, but that tentative observation does not establish successful syllable learning. Correctly continuing English patterns is difficult even when human speakers find the judgments easy.
children: Training on **ten thousand words instead of one thousand**, and continuing for more iterations, are possible extensions that would give the model more opportunities to learn. These changes were proposed, but no completed successful result from them is established.

Architecture specifies the parts of a model, while training determines the weights that make those parts useful. Giving a model heads and layers does not by itself guarantee that it has acquired the intended language patterns.

teaching.text: **Software 1.0 is writing a program in a programming language**, such as Python, C or Pascal. The person specifies the operations the computer should carry out.
children: **Software 2.0 learns a program through a neural network's weights.** Input and output data guide changes to the weights, so the learned mapping carries the information needed to produce outputs from inputs.

**Software 3.0 uses language to instruct an agentic system to construct and run a program.** The English request can specify the model, training data and desired outputs, while the system produces the code and executes the requested work.

**Vibe coding** is this use of natural language to direct program construction and execution. Understanding heads, layers, vectors and learning makes it possible to specify what the requested program should do, rather than asking for an unexplained result.

teaching.text: **An agentic system can build and train a smaller language model from an English instruction.** The system receiving the English instruction and the model being constructed are different levels of the process.
children: The agentic system used its existing language and programming abilities to produce the word-pattern implementation. That implementation was reported to use **NumPy**, numerical Python, and a pronunciation resource.

The smaller model is designed to learn the word patterns through changes to its own weights. Asking an already trained system to build a model is therefore different from assuming that the new model already knows what the larger system knows.

teaching.text: **Claude Shannon's 1948 paper, A Mathematical Theory of Communication, examined how sequences can approximate English.** Unrestricted letter sequences look unlike English, while adding information about the language's patterns can make generated sequences more English-like.
children: The examples progress from strings with implausible combinations toward sequences containing more familiar arrangements and recognizable pieces. Their relevance is that a language imposes structure on what can follow what.

Shannon's examples were statistical approximations of language, rather than modern networks with attention heads and layers. They connect information theory with sequence prediction without making the two methods the same architecture.
